claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation better than homogeneous coatings of similar overall composition.
The proposed multilayer coatings have a nanoscale layered structure with regularly spaced, coherent interfaces.
Coherent interfaces in the multilayer structure impede dislocation motion.
Slower dislocation motion reduces the accumulation of permanent plastic strain.
Reduced dislocation mobility lowers the creep rate relative to a homogeneous coating.
Elevated temperature and constant stress below the yield strength can produce measurable creep in these coatings.
Under matched temperature and stress, the multilayer coating will have a significantly lower creep strain rate than the homogeneous baseline.
Under matched temperature and stress, the multilayer coating will accumulate less plastic deformation than the homogeneous baseline.
The interface-impediment mechanism is expected to dominate when creep is active, particularly at elevated temperatures.
Nanoscale layer thicknesses can maintain coherent interfaces effective at blocking dislocations.
The beneficial interface effect may diminish at very low temperatures.
Severe interfacial degradation may diminish the beneficial interface effect.
The relative contributions of compositional complexity and specific interface characteristics to creep resistance are unresolved.
The relative contributions to creep resistance may vary with processing parameters and operating conditions.
